en: The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Girl Candrottarā, Volume One.
Translated by the Dharma Master Jñānagupta of Central India during the Sui Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Great Forest of Vṛji in the kingdom of Vaiśālī.
In a thatched hut, he was together with five hundred great bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats.

There were also eight thousand bodhisattvas present, all of whom were of great virtue, possessing great majestic power and great supernormal faculties; they had all received and upheld various dhāraṇīs, attained unimpeded eloquence, attained various meditative concentrations, and attained the patience of non-arising. They were fully endowed with the five supernatural powers, their words were truthful and devoid of falsehood, and they remained free from both praise and blame.

They are entirely unattached to their own kin or to material gain; they preach the Dharma to others without seeking recompense; having attained profound *dharmakṣānti*, they are able to cross to the other shore; being fully endowed with fearlessness, they have transcended the works of Māra and are free from the fetters of karma.

They have no doubt or obstruction regarding the nature of all phenomena; having achieved accomplishment through cultivation over immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kalpas, they always comfort practitioners with a pleasing countenance and never knit their brows. With skillful phrases and an unchanging mind, their eloquence is inexhaustible, and they have likewise accomplished the dharma of equanimity.

They are able to preach the Dharma among the great assembly with fearlessness; they can expound a single verse of the Dharma for more than hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, having attained skillful means and inexhaustible wisdom. They know that all things of the three periods of time are like illusions and transformations, and are also like mirages, like the moon reflected in water, like dreams, like stars, and like echoes in an empty valley.

Knowing that the nature of all phenomena is empty, signless, and wishless, their minds are ever in a state of quiescence; abiding in the dharma of suchness, they are free from all grasping and rejecting.

Having attained immeasurable wisdom and skillful means, they also know the activities of the minds of sentient beings and the matters of skillful means; wherever there are those to be transformed, they are able to expound all dharmas accordingly.
They harbor no malice toward the minds of sentient beings and are free from all attachment; being devoid of further afflictions, they are fully endowed with the practice of patience.

They thoroughly understand the nature of all phenomena and have already accomplished the adornment of the Buddha-fields; they constantly achieve the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* (samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha).
Furthermore, they are able to accomplish the exhortation for the wisdom of the Buddhas and can sever the various afflictions and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
They sport within all samādhis and samāpattis;
they are also all able to attain skillful wisdom and expedient means.
Their names are as follows:
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva,
Durlabha Bodhisattva, Gandhahastin Bodhisattva, Anikṣiptadhura Bodhisattva,
Sūryagarbha Bodhisattva, Dhāraṇī Bodhisattva, Gandhaprabhāsa Bodhisattva, and Meghasvara Bodhisattva...
The Bodhisattva Saṃvibhakta-suvarṇaprabhāsa-adhiṣṭhānarāja, the Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa, the Bodhisattva Ratnadhvaja,
the Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, the Bodhisattva Rājavikrīḍita,
the Bodhisattva Priyadarśana, the Bodhisattva Sattvatāraṇa, the Bodhisattva Satatodyukta, and the Bodhisattva Satatasamitābhirata.
The Bodhisattva Mūla, the Bodhisattva Durgatipariśodhana, the Bodhisattva Vajracaraṇa, the Bodhisattva Trailokyacaraṇa,
the Bodhisattva Acalacaryā, the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin, the Bodhisattva Guṇakośa, the Bodhisattva Padmaguṇa,
the Bodhisattva Gandhahastin, and the Bodhisattva Gambhīrajñānapratibhānaprāpta.
...the Bodhisattva Mahāprajñā, the Bodhisattva Dharmottara-jāta, the Bodhisattva Sarvadharmāsaṃśaya-guṇa,
the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrānta-gāmin, the Bodhisattva Sarvabhayavikiraṇa, the Bodhisattva Sarvāvaraṇanirghātana,
the Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda-svara, the Bodhisatva Anabhilāpya, the Bodhisattva Pratibhāna-rāśi, and Maitreya...
With the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas headed by Maitreya as their leaders,
there were likewise hundreds of thousands of such Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas present.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the Kuśa-grass vihāra within the Mahāvana forest at Vaiśālī.

At that time, the kings, ministers, officials, wealthy elders, brahmins, householders, common people, and merchants who had come from afar all paid him their respects, honoring and serving him with reverence.

At that time, there was in that city a Licchavi named Vimalakīrti. His family was immensely wealthy with immeasurable assets; his granaries and treasuries were so full they could not be counted, and all manner of four-footed and two-footed livestock were present in great abundance.
That man had a wife named Vimalā, who was lovely, upright, and beautiful of form, endowed with all the marks of feminine beauty.

At that time, the woman became pregnant, and when the nine months were complete, she gave birth to a daughter whose countenance was upright and beautiful, her body perfectly formed, such that those who beheld her could never tire of looking.
When the girl was born, there was a great radiance that illuminated her home, filling every corner.
At the time of her birth, the earth shook violently, and all the trees outside her house’s gate spontaneously overflowed with ghee.

In the city of Vaiśālī, all the great drums and small drums, as well as various kinds of musical instruments, resounded spontaneously without being played; above, reaching into the void, the heavens rained down a multitude of flowers; and within his residence, hidden treasuries at each of the four corners opened of their own accord, and a variety of subtle and secret jewels all appeared.
When the girl was born, she did not cry; instead, she immediately raised her hands with palms joined and spoke this verse:
"Because I did not commit any evil deeds in the past, I have now obtained such a pure body.
Had I committed evil deeds, I would not have been born into this great and noble family."
Thus, because in the past they severed all evil conduct, were fond of giving, disciplined, and heedful;
and because they honored and revered those worthy of respect, they have now been born into this noble and virtuous family.
I recall in the past, when Kāśyapa Buddha came to Vaiśālī to beg for alms;
from atop my terrace I beheld that Honored One, and having seen him thus, my mind became pure.
Once my mind has attained purity, I shall honor and revere that Tathāgata;
yet at that time, there will be no incense, flowers, unguents, powdered incense, food, or drink.
Then, a voice was heard in the air: "The Buddha seeks no recompense in this world;
out of compassion for all sentient beings, he wanders about to beg for food."
If you wish to make offerings to that Venerable One, you should resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment;
compared to making offerings throughout the three realms, it is not equal to one who develops faith and arouses the mind for the Way.
Having heard such empty sounds, I further beheld the subtle and wondrous marks of the Buddhas;
thereupon I gave rise to the unshakable bodhicitta and leapt from the upper story down to the ground.
Abiding in the air at the height of one *tāla* tree, he again beholds all the Buddhas of the ten directions;
like Mount Sumeru composed of various jewels, so too is the body of Kāśyapa Buddha.
At that time, through the spiritual power of all Buddhas, mandārava flowers filled my hands;
I then scattered them over Kāśyapa, and they immediately formed a pure and wondrous flower canopy.
The Buddhas of the ten directions whom I behold have bodies adorned with subtle and wondrous marks and signs;
I see mandārava flower canopies, which are likewise like those offered by Kāśyapa.
At that time, as I spoke these words in mid-air, I made this vow: "May I become the most supreme among two-legged beings;
even if I must practice for as many eons as there are motes of dust, I shall never retreat from my resolve to attain Bodhi."
Devas, nāgas, and even non-humans— these eight classes of beings, numbering two thousand—
having heard such a lion’s roar from me, have likewise resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta.
Having departed from the Heaven of the Thirty-three, I have returned to be born in Jambudvīpa;
because I have never ceased to practice virtuous conduct, I therefore exhort you all to cultivate meritorious deeds.
When I was in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, I made offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha;
now, in this life, not for the sake of the five desires, I come once more to make offerings to this Tathāgata.
I recall the karmic retributions of my past lives, having passed through eighty-nine places of birth;
the merit I have received is all as it is now—therefore, the wise should offer worship to the Buddha.
When she had spoken these verses, the maiden remained silent.

Due to the causal conditions of various roots of goodness she had cultivated in the past, her body spontaneously became adorned with celestial garments and robes of exquisite jewels; from her person issued a wondrous radiance surpassing the light of the moon, like the luster of gold illuminating the interior of her home.
Because her parents had seen that light, they immediately gave her the name Candrottarā.

Not long after Candrottarā was born, her body suddenly became as large as that of an eight-year-old girl. Wherever she walked, stood, sat, or remained, the ground there was entirely radiant with brilliant light. From all the pores of her body issued the fragrance of sandalwood, and the breath from her mouth was as fragrant as an utpala lotus.

All the sons of the Kṣatriya kings, princes, and their younger brothers in the city of Vaiśālī, as well as the ministers, householders, elders, brahmins, and other youths of noble and prominent lineages, heard from afar of that maiden Candrottarā’s reputation for being beautiful, lovely, and peerless in the world. Having heard this, they were all set ablaze by the fire of desire; their minds were filled with feverish distress that pervaded their entire bodies, and each of them thought:
"May I obtain that maiden Candrottarā as my wife."

At that time, after all the youths had formed this thought, they all went to the house of the Licchavi Vimalakīrti to announce their intentions and pay their respects; each of them promised to provide immeasurable treasures, such as camels, donkeys, elephants, horses, and various other goods.
Some, upon meeting the Licchavi, threatened him verbally, saying:
"We shall seize and plunder [them]!"
Some shouted and spoke thus:

"If you do not give us your daughter now, we shall certainly plunder your beds, bedding, furniture, wealth, clothing, and all the various necklaces upon your body; we will take away all your ornaments and attire."
Some said they would beat him, while others said they would bind him; they informed him of such terrifying matters.
At that time, Vimalakīrti the Licchavi felt terror arise in his heart; his hair stood on end and he was filled with sorrow and distress, thinking to himself:
"Perhaps they will use their power to forcibly seize my daughter Candrottarā and carry her away."
"Or perhaps there is someone who wishes to come and take my life.

However, that Licchavi lost his composure; distressed and tormented, with knitted brows and furrowed cheeks, he stared at his daughter without blinking, and immediately raised his voice in a wailing cry, shedding tears like falling rain.
At that time, Candrottarā, seeing her father thus grieving and weeping, asked him:
"Father, for what reason are you now so distressed and weeping?"
At that time, the Licchavi Vimalakīrti said to his daughter, "Do you not know what has happened today?
Because of your body, all the people within the city have formed hostile bonds with me; therefore, each of them wishes to come and contend for you."
"I fear that now, by their power, you will be abducted and taken away; my life and all my wealth and treasures will be lost.
At that time, Candrottarā replied to her father in verse:
"Even if all sentient beings throughout the entire land of Jambudvīpa..."
Each possesses strength like that of Nārāyaṇa, and every person holds a sharp blade and weapon in hand;
though they exhaust all their physical power to pursue me, they will ultimately be unable to harm me.
My heart of loving-kindness cannot be harmed by poisonous weapons, nor can I be swept away by water or fire.
One does not fear corpses, various ghosts, or those who utter curses;
with a resolute mind of loving-kindness free from anger, one ultimately fears no other through that very compassion.
Now that I have given rise to this mind of loving-kindness, protecting the world as if protecting my own body;
since I do not inflict suffering upon others even in the present, who then could possibly harm me?
Having grown weary of desire, I myself am free from the perception of desire; having perfected loving-kindness, I am likewise free from ill will and delusion.
Since I am without the afflictions of lust, hatred, and folly, no one is able to harm me.
I observe all sentient beings, regarding them all as my own parents;
in this world, one who possesses such compassion can certainly not be deceived by others.
Even if space were to sink into the earth, And Mount Sumeru were to enter a mustard seed;
Even if the waters of the four great oceans were to dwell within a cow’s footprint, Still, none could ever subdue my body.
At that time, having spoken these verses, Candrottarā addressed her parents, saying:
"Venerable parents!
If such a thing must indeed come to pass, I pray that you ring the bells at the crossroads of this city of Vaiśālī and issue a proclamation to all the people within the city, saying as follows:"
"From now, after seven days, my daughter Candrāvatī shall certainly go forth to seek a husband for herself and choose a spouse.
All you men who are as yet unmarried should each adorn yourselves well with fine garments and necklaces;

you must also sweep the streets and alleys within the city and scatter fragrant flowers, and prepare incense sticks, powdered incense, flower garlands, and all other such items. Furthermore, erect precious banners and suspend streamers and canopies."
"Having thus adorned herself with various beautiful ornaments and employing these diverse methods, she requested her parents to perform this task.

At that time, having heard the daughter's words, the parents accepted her speech and went out from their home. Following what the daughter had said, they immediately shook their bells and announced to all the people within the city, saying:
"My daughter, Candrottarā!..."
From this day forth, for seven days, you shall go out from your homes to seek marriage and choose a husband.

You should each exert yourselves to adorn your clothing and sweep and clean the streets. Prepare and arrange incense flowers, burning incense, and powdered incense; erect precious banners, pennants, and canopies; and thus adorn yourselves in various such beautiful ways.

At that time, all the people within the city, having heard these words, felt their hearts leap with joy; each, at the gates and courtyards of their respective homes as well as in the streets and alleys, adorned them with splendor and magnificence exceeding what had been described.

At that time, within the city, the Kṣatriya ministers, Brahmins, householders, elders, and even the artisans—all the young men—washed their hair, bathed their bodies, and anointed them with exquisite perfumes. Each vied with the others to adorn themselves with fine garments and various necklaces. Having done so, they then addressed their surrounding retinues, saying:
"You must not let your minds waver; do not give rise to other thoughts."
"If that girl Candrottarā does not come to me of her own accord, you must all use force to assist me in seizing her.

Then, on the sixth day following, at the time of the full moon on the fifteenth day, having observed the eightfold fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa), she spent that clear and tranquil night walking back and forth in meditation upon the upper terrace.
By the Buddha's supernatural power, there suddenly emerged from his right hand a lotus flower: its stem was of gold, its petals of silver, its filaments of lapis lazuli, and its pericarp of agate.

The flower has exactly one hundred petals; its radiance is brilliant and its essence exquisite and beautiful. Within the flower is the image of a Tathāgata sitting in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), his body appearing naturally golden in color. His majestic light is magnificent and brightly illuminates that pavilion; he is adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor characteristics.
The light emanating from that image of the Tathāgata likewise shone everywhere throughout the interior of Candrottarā’s home.

At that time, as Candrottarā suddenly beheld the flower in her own right hand, she gazed up at the form of the Tathāgata; with joy and exultation overflowing her entire being, she could not contain herself. She then addressed the manifested image of the Tathāgata in verse, saying:
"I wonder, O Benevolent One, are you a deva or a nāga, Or perhaps a kiṃnara, a yakṣa, or the like?"
Are you a ghost, a spirit, or an asura?
I pray that you, O Mass of Virtue, will explain this to me.
Venerable One, this body of yours is inconceivable, like the golden sun and other celestial bodies.
Or again, he may manifest a body of yellow hue, suddenly appearing like crystal or a reddish-pale color.
I have no conceptual thoughts regarding his body or mind; seeing the Venerable One’s merit, I am filled with great joy.
O Benevolent One, by whom are you now sent?
I do not yet know from what direction you have come;
I am unaware for what purpose you have come;
and having arrived, where do you intend to go?
“His majesty is as brilliant as a mass of fire, His merit is as towering as Mount Sumeru.
At that time, the manifested image of the Tathāgata again addressed the girl Candrottarā in verse:
“I am now neither a deva nor a nāga, Nor am I a yakṣa or a gandharva;”
The World-Honored Buddha, the Lion of the Śākya clan, has now sent me to your presence.
Therefore, I am not a deva, a nāga, or a yakṣa;
I am neither a human nor a kiṃnara, nor one of the eight classes of beings such as the mahoragas—I am truly a messenger of the Buddha, the Lion of the Śākya clan.
At that time, Candrottarā again addressed the manifested image of the Tathāgata in verse, speaking these words:
"The Buddha, the World-Honored One, of whom you now speak— What is his physical form and body like?"
"Please describe his form and appearance for me, so that having heard it, I may contemplate it accordingly.
Furthermore, you yourself claim to be an emissary of our Buddha’s Dharma, yet you do not describe the Buddha’s marks for me.
When I observe your majesty and your supernormal powers, they are peerless in the world and truly like those of a Buddha."
At that time, the manifested image of the Tathāgata replied to the girl Candrottarā in verse:
“The body of that Honored One is the color of pure gold, Endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man;
He is able to serve as a field of merit for all sentient beings, And for this reason, his name is called ‘Buddha.’”
He is able to personally awaken to all phenomena, and furthermore discerns the minds of sentient beings—whether superior, middling, or inferior; for this reason, he is named Buddha.
He fully understands all worldly affairs, And thoroughly comprehends all phenomena;
Having known all phenomena, he has reached the further shore— Therefore, his name is called Buddha.
Regarding the minds of all sentient beings, one’s own mind can know and see each one;
yet with respect to both the sentient beings and their minds, one remains unstained and unattached in both respects.

By practicing generosity, he attained Buddhahood; likewise, by constantly upholding the pure precepts, and further through patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, he achieved enlightenment.
There is nothing among worldly affairs that he does not know—namely, all arts and crafts;
constantly harboring the minds of compassion, joy, and equanimity, for this reason his title is called Buddha.
Having subdued all the māras and their like, his fame resounds throughout ten million worlds;
having awakened to the unsurpassed path by himself, for this reason he is named Buddha.
In the past, he was ever able to turn the supreme wheel of all dharmas;
his radiance universally illumined ten million lands, and he constantly preached suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
There are thousands of Buddha-fields, numbering in the hundreds, billions, and nayutas;
because his vast tongue can cover them all, he is therefore named "Buddha."
There are thousands of Buddha-fields, their number like the sands of the Ganges;
he utters a great sound that completely fills them all, and for this reason his name is called "Buddha."
Thousands of billions of Buddha-fields, those Honored Ones can grasp and hold with their hands;
remaining unmoving for ten million *kalpas*, for this reason they are named Buddhas.
Within thousands of billions of Buddha-fields, there are all the Mount Sumerus that exist therein;
having bound them together with a single hair, that Honored One can carry them and travel to as many as billions of fields.
Having heard the sublime phrases of the Buddhas of the past, He attained mastery over the Dharma and crossed to the other shore;
Having realized it through his own awakening, he is able to deliver all beings— For this reason, his name is called Buddha.
Fully endowed with the ten powers of mastery, And further having accomplished the four fearlessnesses;
Having no doubt regarding any of the Buddha-dharmas, For this reason, his name is called "Buddha."
The Buddha has no one to perform his consecration; he is fully endowed with the accomplishment of the five eyes.
The five faculties and five powers are perfectly complete, and the path of the seven factors of enlightenment is free from defilement and attachment.
Well-observing the precepts and dwelling in harmony, Tranquil, disciplined, and most peerless;
Without flattery or crookedness, with a mind that is compliant and harmonious— For this reason, his name is called Buddha.
The Buddha constantly enters all meditative absorptions; his mind is never for a moment distracted, nor does he have fear.
He benefits sentient beings by speaking at the appropriate time; for this reason, his title is "Buddha."
Fully endowed with all merits, he is honored equally by all sentient beings;
possessing all-encompassing wisdom and seeing all phenomena, for this reason his name is called Buddha.
If I were to speak for an eon, or even for hundreds of thousands of millions of eons,
why is it that his name is called "Buddha"?
Because his qualities cannot be fully described, he is named Buddha.

At that time, having heard these verses, Candrottarā was filled with such overwhelming joy and exultation that it pervaded her entire body; she could not contain herself, and a deep longing arose in her heart to behold the Tathāgata.
Again, he addressed the manifested image in verse, saying:
"The Venerable One has thus described these merits; May I now see them? Is it possible?"
If a wise person hears such a Dharma as this, they will certainly find no pleasure in dwelling at home.
If I do not see the Buddha now, I shall surely neither drink nor eat;
I shall likewise take no delight in sleep, nor shall I sit upon my own bed or mat.
Having seen the Venerable One, I am filled with joy; hearing further of his virtues, my mind has attained purity.
If I were to behold the physical marks of that Buddha in person, I would surely give rise once more to a heart of great rapture.
A Buddha, a Great Being, is difficult to hear of in this world, occurring only once in hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas;
I have now heard the name of this One Whose Outflows Are Exhausted—where does that Honored One dwell at present?
The emanated Tathāgata replied:
"The Dharma King now resides within the Great Forest;
his retinue numbers in the hundreds of thousands, all pure, free from defilement, and utterly courageous."
Each is able to bear a trichiliocosm, holding it aloft in their hands for kalpas without fatigue;
having attained concentration, wisdom, and unimpeded eloquence, they possess vast learning like the great ocean.
Through supernormal powers, one can reach billions of lands, Traveling for an entire morning to pay homage to all those Buddhas;
Having made offerings to ten million Buddhas, One returns once again in a single moment.
Without the notion of self or the notion of a Buddha, without the notion of a realm or the notion of a Dharma;
with all notions entirely free from defilement, they bring benefit to all sentient beings.
If you wish to see that World-Honored One, As well as the assembly of great Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas;
And to hear the subtle and wondrous teachings of all Buddhas, Go quickly to the presence of that Great Teacher.
At that time, Candrottarā took hold of that lotus and the emanated Buddha and descended from the pavilion, proceeding to the side of her parents.
Having arrived, she spoke a verse to her parents, saying:
"Parents, behold the flower I hold, Its subtle stem and stalk the color of diamond; The petals are like the moon’s radiance, And its fragrance is most exquisite."
Furthermore, regarding those within the unsurpassed flowers: their various marks are as majestic as the king of mountains.
Such a subtle, wondrous, and most supreme Honored One—who could possibly not make offerings?
I now see throughout the entire house a golden radiance; O Mother, you should know this.
Her body cannot be measured in its entirety, for in an instant it transforms into various colors—red, white, yellow, purple, and crystal. We must now prepare an offering for her.
The Great Sage Gautama is in the Great Forest; quickly take flowers, incense, and powdered incense.
Go together with our parents to present these offerings, and you shall obtain immeasurable merit.
Upon hearing this, the parents exclaimed, "Excellent!
These words of Candrottarā are of great benefit.
They then prepared various kinds of incense and the like, as well as precious banners, streamers, parasols, and flower garlands.
The parents and kinsmen of Candrottara were all dressed in exquisite, superior garments;
with priceless jewels and music, every kind of adornment was fully provided.
Having made these preparations, she departed from her home, intending to go to the Great Forest to the presence of the World-Honored One.
At that time, on the seventh day, six days having already passed, it was the very day Candralekhā had appointed.
At that time, there was a great assembly of immeasurable thousands who gathered together to behold Candrottarā.
Among the crowd, some had come to the assembly with minds afflicted by desire;

others had come to see the city of Vaiśālī, to observe all its adornments—the defensive towers and battlements, the *nirghātaka* windows, the balustrades, the carved rafters, and the various decorative carvings upon the city walls.
At that time, there were immeasurable men and women who, while traveling through that city, came to gaze upon Candrottarā.

Then Candrottarā still held that flower; her parents and their retinue, carrying various flower garlands, ointments, powdered incense, diverse kinds of burning incense, and exquisite garments, as well as precious banners, flags, and canopies, accompanied by various musical sounds, emerged from their home and proceeded through the streets and alleys, surrounded on all sides by attendants.

At that time, when Candrottarā and her retinue went out into the streets and walked along, immeasurable and boundless thousands of people, seeing Candrottarā moving through the streets, immediately approached her and each cried out these words:
"This is my wife! This is my wife!"
At that time, within the great city of Vaiśālī, there were some people who came running all at once, crying out in loud voices toward Candrottarā.

Seeing that the great multitude was approaching with such speed, she immediately soared into the air to the height of a *tāla* tree; holding the flower, she remained suspended in mid-air and addressed the great assembly in verse:
“Behold this wondrous body of mine, Resplendent like refined gold glowing with the hue of fire;”
It is not because of having previously given rise to a lustful mind That one can obtain such a subtle and wondrous body.
Having abandoned sensual desire as if it were a pit of fire, And being unstained by attachment to worldly affairs;
Being able to practice asceticism to discipline the six sense faculties, And practicing all pure brahmacarya.
Seeing the wives and concubines of others, one does not harbor greedy desires, but regards them all as sisters or mothers;
thus one shall be born with a body that inspires joy, which the multitude delights to behold without ever being satiated.
From the pores of my body a wondrous fragrance issues forth; do you not perceive it filling this city?
This is not obtained through the perfuming of lustful desire, but is entirely the fruit of generosity and self-discipline.
I have never had a mind of lust from the very beginning; do not give rise to desire toward me who am free from it.
This honored image now bears witness for me, that my truthful words are without falsehood.
"Among you, some were once my fathers, and I was once your mother;
we have been each other's parents and brothers—how can you give rise to lustful thoughts toward one another?"
I may have killed you all in the past, or perhaps you have come to kill me;
having each acted as an enemy and slain one another, how can you conceive thoughts of desire toward them?
One does not attain physical beauty through desire; one who possesses desire will certainly give rise to unwholesome states.
One whose mind is possessed by desire finds no liberation; therefore, one must now abandon the mind of desire.
If one falls into the hells or among the hungry ghosts, Or into the various species of animals,
As kumbhāṇḍas, yakṣas, asuras, Or piśācas and the like— all are caused by desire.
Blind, tongueless, lame, and deaf, with bodies and forms entirely hideous—
all such various faults and evils arise from a mind of excessive desire in past karma.
If one becomes a Wheel-Turning King in a future life, or Śakra, the Lord of the Thirty-three Heavens,
or Mahābrahmā, Īśvara, and other such deities, it is all due to having extensively practiced pure brahmacarya.
Born blind, mute, and deprived of their true nature, As pigs, dogs, horses, donkeys, and camels,
Or as elephants, oxen, tigers, flies, mosquitoes, and gadflies— All these retributions are obtained through excessive desire.
Born into families of great lords, joy, and happiness—among wealthy elders and householders—all such as these are due to practicing the holy life;
they obtain joy in the present and constantly experience bliss.
Carrying heavy burdens, boiling, roasting, and smoke熏ning the nose; shackles, fetters, cangues, and the physical humiliation of being beaten;
being cut, maimed, castrated, or having one's eyes gouged out—all such service as a slave for others arises from desire.
Whether one wishes to become a pratyekabuddha or an arhat, Or to manifest the bodies of all Buddhas adorned with the various marks;
To awaken oneself and awaken others for the sake of vast benefit— All these arise from abandoning thoughts of desire and existence.
The pursuit of sensual desires is not merely a single affliction; it brings many evils and no benefit.
Those who swiftly hope for liberation from all desires, come with me to the presence of the Tathāgata.
There is no refuge capable of uprooting transgressions, Save for the Buddhas, the Honored Ones among gods and humans;
You should all go swiftly to those Honored Ones, For a Buddha is difficult to behold throughout immeasurable eons.

When Candralekhā had thus spoken these verses to the people, at that moment the great earth shook in its entirety. Within the void of space, immeasurable sons of the gods raised their voices in loud cries, brandishing their robes and dancing; they sang and whistled in countless and innumerable ways, raining down hundreds and thousands of celestial flowers, and performing musical performances beyond description.
At that time, having seen and heard this, the great assembly conceived a sense of weary detachment from all desires, giving rise to thoughts of rarity and of what had never before occurred.

At that moment, the hair on their bodies stood on end; they were no longer troubled by desire, nor did they harbor anger, malice, greed, or delusion; they were without wrath, envy, jealousy, or contention. Free from further afflictions and the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), their bodies were moistened with joy. Each of them mutually conceived thoughts of the other as parents, brothers, sisters, kinsmen, elders, and superiors.
Having completely abandoned all afflictions, they each bowed their heads at the feet of Candrottarā.
At that time, the great assembly took up incense, flowers, powdered incense, ointments, flower garlands, robes, various necklaces, and so forth, and scattered them all toward Candrottarā.
Once they had been scattered and cast away, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, those objects formed a single parasol above the emanated Tathāgata there, half a yojana in width.

At that time, Candrottarā descended from the sky to a height of four finger-widths above the ground; treading through the air, she walked back and forth, and in a brief moment, she emerged from the city of Vaiśālī, intending to go to where the Śākya Tathāgata was.
At that time, the ground shook wherever Candrottarā set her feet; and that great assembly, numbering eighty-four thousand people, followed behind Candrottarā as they proceeded in succession.

At that time, the Elder Śāriputra, together with five hundred bhikṣus, dressed himself in the morning, took up his robes and bowl, and set out for the city of Vaiśālī for the purpose of begging for alms.
At that time, the assembly of those śrāvakas saw Candrottarā from afar, surrounded by her great retinue, approaching toward them.
Śāriputra then addressed the elder Mahākāśyapa, saying:
"Elder Kāśyapa!..."

"The one who has come is the maiden Candrottarā, who intends to go before the Buddha. Let us first question her; by examining her meaning and intent, we shall test whether or not she has attained forbearance."
At that time, the elder Śāriputra and five hundred bhikṣus proceeded forward until they reached the side of the girl Candrottarā. Having arrived, they said to her:
"Where do you intend to go now?"
The girl Candrottarā then replied to the Elder Śāriputra:
"Venerable Śāriputra!
Since you have now questioned me with these words, where do you intend to go?"
"I am now departing just as Śāriputra has departed; it is simply a departure like that!
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed Candrottarā with these words:
"I wish to enter the city of Vaiśālī, yet you are now departing from it; how can you say: 'I am now departing just as Śāriputra has departed; it is simply a departure like that'?"
"Am I now departing in the same manner as Śāriputra departed?
At that time, Candrottarā replied again to the Elder Śāriputra, saying:
"Indeed, Śāriputra!"
"On what basis do you lift and set down your feet?
Śāriputra replied,
"Now, as I lift my feet and set them down, they both rest upon empty space."
The girl replied again to Śāriputra: "I am also like this;
when I lift my foot and set it down, both actions entirely depend upon empty space, yet the realm of empty space does not form any discrimination. Therefore, I say:
'Just as the Venerable Śāriputra goes, so do I go.'"
“Venerable Śāriputra!
Let this matter be so for now; what practice is Śāriputra currently engaged in?
Śāriputra replied:
"I am practicing toward Nirvana in this manner.
The woman spoke again to Śāriputra, saying:
"Venerable Śāriputra!..."
"Are not all dharmas directed toward the practice of Nirvāṇa? I, too, am now proceeding toward that same destination.
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra again addressed Candrottarā with these words:
"If all dharmas are directed toward Nirvāṇa, why is it that you have not yet entered parinirvāṇa?"
The woman replied:
"Venerable Śāriputra!
If one were to head toward nirvāṇa, one would not attain parinirvāṇa."

Why is this? Because the practice of nirvāṇa is neither arising nor ceasing; the practitioner of nirvāṇa cannot be perceived, for its essence is non-discriminatory and there is nothing therein to be extinguished. By this principle, the one who practices for nirvāṇa is itself nirvāṇa.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed Candrottarā, saying:
"Which vehicle do you currently practice?
Do you practice the Śrāvaka vehicle?"
"Are you practicing the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas,
or are you practicing the Mahāyāna?
At that time, Candrottarā replied to Śāriputra with these words:
"Venerable Śāriputra!
Since you have now asked me which vehicle I practice, I shall in turn question you, Venerable Śāriputra; I only pray that you will answer me as you see fit."
Regarding the Dharma realized by Śāriputra: does he practice the Śrāvaka vehicle,
the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the Mahāyāna?
At that time, Śāriputra again replied to the girl with these words:
"It is not so, Candrottarā! Why is this?"
"However, that Dharma is without anything to be discriminated and is beyond verbal expression;
it is neither distinct nor one, nor is it manifold. At that time, Candrottarā replied to the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:

"Therefore, one should not discriminate among phenomena. Whether they have a single characteristic or different characteristics, there are no distinct characteristics; within all characteristics, there is nothing upon which to dwell. Thus, in Nirvāṇa, there is truly nothing to be extinguished."
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra again addressed Candrottarā, saying:
"How extraordinary, how extraordinary!
You are now able to possess such eloquence, free from all obstruction. Therefore, how many Buddhas have you served in the past?"
At that time, Candrottarā replied to Śāriputra, saying:
"Venerable Śāriputra!
Regarding your question to me as to how many Buddhas you have previously served, it is like the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu)."
Then Śāriputra again asked the girl:
"As for what you call the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), how much do they comprise?
The girl replied once more:
"It is as if there is no difference between ignorance (*avidyā*), existence (*bhava*), and craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Then Śāriputra again asked the woman:
"How many kinds of ignorance, existence, and craving are there?"
The girl replied,
"It is no different from the realm of sentient beings.
Then Śāriputra again asked the girl:
"How vast is the realm of sentient beings?
The girl replied,
"It is as vast as the sphere of activity of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present."
Śāriputra said, "If this is so,
what is it that you have spoken, and what is its explanation?
The girl replied:
“I shall answer according to what the Venerable One has asked.
Then Śāriputra again asked the woman,
“What is the meaning of my question?”
The girl replied,
"I am asking about words. Śāriputra said:
"When those words have ceased, there is no trace left behind.
The girl replied,
"Venerable Śāriputra!"
"In this manner, among all phenomena characterized by cessation, whether there be one who asks or one who answers, both are characterized by cessation and are unobtainable.

At that time, the Elder Śāriputra again addressed Candrottarā with these words:
"At this moment, you possess such marks of patience within the stage of a bodhisattva; it will not be long before you attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
At that time, Candrottarā spoke these words:
"Venerable Śāriputra!
Awakening is beyond verbal expression; it is spoken of only by means of provisional names and letters!"
That which is called "accomplishment" is also spoken of as a mere conventional designation; whether long or short, both are simply names.
Venerable sir, why do you speak in this way?
"You shall before long attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Venerable Śāriputra!
As for that which is Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, it has no place of arising and cannot be described; it possesses no intrinsic nature, and within it there is likewise nothing that can be accomplished.
"Why is this? Because the essence of bodhi has no dual characteristics; therefore, bodhi is non-dual and free from unity.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the girl Candrottarā, saying these words:
“You should now first proceed to where the Buddha is; we shall return to that place shortly to listen to the Dharma.”
At that time, Candrottarā again addressed the Elder Śāriputra, saying:
"Venerable Śāriputra!
The Tathāgata does not speak for those who merely listen to the Dharma, nor does he speak for those who merely delight in the Dharma."
Śāriputra said,
"If that is so for the Tathāgata, for whom does he preach the Dharma?
The girl replied:
“Venerable Śāriputra!
If, upon hearing anything, one does not give rise to thoughts of attachment nor thoughts of delight, it is for such a person that the Tathāgata thus preaches the Dharma.
At that time, Śāriputra again spoke to Candrottarā as follows:
"If there are sentient beings who approach the Buddha to hear the Dharma, for the sake of hearing that Dharma, would the Tathāgata not then preach the Dharma for them?
At that time, Candrottarā replied to him again:
"If there are sentient beings who form such a thought as 'This is the Tathāgata preaching the Dharma for me,' such sentient beings abide in the notion of a self (ātman)."

"If there were those who had truly and penetratingly entered into the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), they would have no such thought, and would never say, 'The Buddha has taught such a Dharma for our sake.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the Elder Śāriputra, saying:
"Venerable Śāriputra!..."

"Since this woman has now approached the presence of the Buddha, there will surely be great Dharma and meaning today. We too may turn back and depart; it would be better for us not to eat today than to have our bodies remain outside and fail to hear such Dharma and meaning."
"Therefore, those śrāvakas immediately turned back and followed Candrottarā toward the place where the Buddha was.

At that time, Candrottarā gradually proceeded to the grass-thatched hut within that great forest; having reached the Buddha’s presence, she prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and took the incense, flowers, powdered incense, ointments, robes, wealth, precious banners, flags, and canopies she had brought for the Buddha and scattered them over him, scattering them again and again."
At that time, the great assembly also scattered incense, flowers, floral garlands, ointments, and powdered incense upon the Buddha; having scattered them once, they scattered them again.
The various flowers thus scattered formed a single flower-canopy above the Buddha’s head, its length and breadth covering and filling ten *yojanas*.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the girl Candrottarā, saying:
"From where did you relinquish your body in the past to come and be born here?"
"When this body is cast off, where will I be reborn?
The woman replied, "Mañjuśrī!..."
"What do you think?
From where did this image of the Tathāgata that I now hold, seated upon a lotus, relinquish its body to come and be born here? And after relinquishing this body, where will it be reborn?"
Mañjuśrī spoke again to Candrottarā:
"This is merely a transformation!
Now, that which is called a 'transformation' has no place where it casts off the body, nor does it have any subsequent birth."
The girl replied: "So it is, so it is, Mañjuśrī!"
“The fundamental nature of all phenomena is transformation; regarding those phenomena, I perceive neither a time of cessation nor a time of arising.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin spoke thus to the girl Candrottarā:
“So it is, Candrottarā!”
"Since it is impossible to attain Buddhahood in a female body, why do you not now transform your female body?
The woman replied,
"O son of good family!..."
"Indeed, the essence of emptiness neither revolves nor transforms; all dharmas are likewise so.
How then can I transform this female body?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara again addressed Candrottarā with these words:
“Have you ever seen the Tathāgata before?
The girl replied, “Noble son!”
"I see the Tathāgata as being no different from the emanated Buddha held in my hand.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Saṃgharakṣita again addressed Candrottarā, saying:
"Are you now able to discern the meaning of the Dharma?"
At that time, the woman replied: "Good son!
The essence of the dharma-realm cannot be described in words, nor can it be encompassed by letters, calculation, or enumeration."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Unobstructed Eloquence again addressed Candrottarā, saying:
"What teachings did you hear from the presence of the Tathāgatas of the past?"
The woman replied, "Good son!
Now look up at the space above; the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is equal to this space and no different from it, and those who hear it are likewise so."
“Good son! Those characteristics of phenomena are like space—without difference and without distinction.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha addressed the girl, saying:
“What manner of offerings did you present to the Buddhas of the past?
How did you dedicate those merits? The girl replied:
“Good son! As for the merit obtained by my giving this emanated Buddha image to that Buddha and his Saṃgha, what is its nature?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja replied to Candrottarā:
"This Buddha is an emanation; if one gives to him, there would be no characteristic of merit.
The girl replied, "Noble son!
I am also like this: regarding the acts of giving and the dedications I performed before the Tathāgatas of former days, I likewise manifest these signs and likewise perform such dedications.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Undiminished-Mind spoke again, saying:
"How is it that you are now able to extend a mind of loving-kindness universally toward all sentient beings?"
The girl replied, "Noble son!
They are no different from those sentient beings."
The Bodhisattva spoke again:
"What is the nature of those sentient beings?
The woman replied once more:
"The affairs of sentient beings are neither of the past, nor of the future, nor of the present;
and that mind of loving-kindness is likewise so, not comprised within the past, the future, or the present;
furthermore, it cannot be expressed in words."
"Noble son! Such was the nature of that practice of loving-kindness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King of Joy again addressed the woman, saying these words:
“Have you now attained the Dharma-eye?
The woman replied, “Virtuous man! [I have.]”
"I do not yet possess even the fleshly eye, much less the Dharma-eye.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Resolute Mind again addressed the girl, saying these words:
"How long has it been since you set out on the path of bodhi?"
The girl replied, "Noble son!
Just as it has been since that mirage appeared, so too has it been since I first resolved upon Bodhicitta."
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the girl, saying:
"When will you attain the realization of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
The girl replied, "It shall be just as with Maitreya Bodhisattva; when will he transcend the stage of the conduct of ordinary beings?
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is rare indeed that this woman possesses such eloquence.
How is it that she is able to engage in dialogue with such great dragons clad in armor, standing upright without sitting and without bowing her body to pay homage to these bodhisattvas?”
At that time, Candrottarā addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"Venerable Śāriputra!
Just as a small fire, by its very nature of burning, is able to burn all things whatsoever."
"So it is, so it is! Venerable Śāriputra!

Bodhisattvas are no different from the Buddhas; when they wish to incinerate all afflictions among all conditioned phenomena, there are no afflictions—whether their own or those of others—that they cannot burn away."
At that time, Śāriputra again asked the girl:
"When you have attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, what will that buddha-field be like?"
The girl replied, "Venerable Śāriputra!

In my future buddha-field, there shall be no one with such limited conduct and meager wisdom, nor any of such narrow and inferior reputation as you, Śāriputra, are today; I shall certainly take hold of such a buddha-field."
At that time, Śāriputra spoke again to Candrottarā:
"Since you have already stated that the entire dharma-realm and the essence of the Tathāgata are equal and without distinction,
what then is the difference between what is seen now and what is superior?"
The girl Candrottarā said:
"Venerable Śāriputra!

It is like the great ocean and a cow’s footprint; although the water in those two is equal and no different, that cow’s footprint cannot receive immeasurable and boundless sentient beings in the way that the great ocean can."
"So it is, so it is! Venerable Śāriputra!
Although the śrāvakas of the Buddhas share the same dharma-realm, the śrāvakas cannot bring about such great benefit for immeasurable and boundless multitudes of sentient beings as do the Buddhas."
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
For example, there is empty space within a mustard seed, and there is also empty space in the worlds of the ten directions; although these two spaces are not different from one another.

However, the space within a mustard seed cannot contain villages or cities, nor can it establish Mount Sumeru or the great oceans, appearing as if it were the empty space of the worlds of the ten directions.
"So it is, so it is! Venerable Śāriputra!
Although they are alike in being empty, signless, and wishless, there are distinctions between the Buddhas and the śrāvakas."

However, those śrāvakas are unable to bring great benefit to those immeasurable and boundless multitudes of sentient beings in the same manner as the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra said:
"It is so, Candrottarā!
Is not the liberation attained by the Buddha and his śrāvakas equal?"
Candrottarā replied:
"Venerable Śāriputra!
Do not speak thus, saying that the liberation of the Buddhas and that of the śrāvakas is equal."
Then Śāriputra again asked the girl,
“What are the characteristics of such a matter?
The girl replied once more:
“Venerable Śāriputra!
I now wish to ask something; please explain it to me according to your understanding.
When you realized the liberation of mind, were you able to make this trichiliocosm world as level as the palm of a hand?”
Have all the trees and mountains already bowed down toward you?
And has it been possible to utterly eliminate all evils?
Has he completely eliminated the afflictions of all sentient beings?
Has he been prostrated to by all the devas?
Has a host of Māras gathered and filled an area of thirty yojanas come before him?
"Has there ever been even a single thought that gave rise to wisdom and attained liberation?
Furthermore, has it ever been possible to subdue all the retinues of Māra?
At that time, Śāriputra replied to the girl Candrottarā, saying these words:
"I do not possess even one such thing among all these matters.
The girl spoke again:
"Venerable Śāriputra!..."
When a bodhisattva is at the site of enlightenment, they are able to perform such supreme and wondrous deeds, and there are furthermore immeasurable and boundless superior deeds.
Venerable Śāriputra!

Between the liberation of the śrāvakas and the liberation of the Buddhas, there exist such distinctions of victory and defeat, superiority and inferiority; how can you, Venerable One, entertain the thought that the liberation of the Buddha-Tathāgata is equal to that of the śrāvakas?
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the girl Candrottarā, saying:
"Excellent, excellent,
Candrottarā!"
"It is indeed fitting that you are now able to speak with such unimpeded eloquence.

At that moment, the manifested image of the Tathāgata held in the right hand of Candrottarā rose from the flower and proceeded to where the World-Honored One was. Having circumambulated the World-Honored One three times, it entered through his navel; by the Buddha’s supernatural power, the great earth shook violently.

At that time, from each and every pore of the World-Honored One’s body, there emerged a lotus flower, its color like pure gold, with petals of white silver and a lotus pedestal made of jewels from the treasury of merit.
Within each of those flowers, there spontaneously appeared another Buddha, seated in the full lotus posture.

The emanated forms of those Tathāgatas, adorned with all the marks of excellence, pervaded the Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions, manifesting themselves naturally to preach the Dharma to those beings.
The Dharma phrases spoken in those various Buddha-fields, through the supernatural power of the Buddhas, were heard again in this Tathāgata’s land.
At that time, Candrottarā, seeing such wondrous and supreme supernormal powers, was filled with such exuberant joy that it pervaded her entire body, which she could not contain.
The lotus flower held in her right hand was then seized and hurled toward the body of the Tathāgata; once it reached him, it remained above the Buddha’s crown, forming a floral canopy.
The canopy was square and regular, supported by four pillars below; its length and breadth were perfectly equal, as if marked by a carpenter’s line.
Within the canopy, a seat spontaneously manifested, adorned with various jewels, and covered with immeasurable celestial garments.
At that moment, there suddenly appeared upon that seat another manifested image of a Buddha, resembling Śākyamuni, sitting cross-legged with distinct clarity.
When the girl Candrottarā threw those flowers, she made this aspiration:
"World-Honored One!

By the power of the causal conditions of these roots of goodness, may I, in future ages, for the sake of all sentient beings who dwell in the notion of a self, preach the Dharma to them so that they may eliminate the notion of a self."

At that time, through the Buddha’s supernatural power, a second lotus suddenly appeared in her right hand. She then took that flower and threw it toward the Tathāgata; once it reached him, it remained above the Tathāgata as a second canopy, adorned with various jewels as described above.
Then that woman spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
By means of these roots of goodness, may I, in future ages, preach the Dharma for those sentient beings who abide in the view of self, so that they may eliminate their attachment to self."

At that time, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, a third lotus suddenly appeared in her right hand. The woman then took this flower and threw it toward the Tathāgata; it immediately transformed into a third flower-canopy, adorned with various jewels as described above.
At that time, the woman spoke again:
"World-Honored One!

By means of these roots of goodness and their causal conditions, may I, in future ages, for those sentient beings who dwell in all conceptual marks, preach the Dharma to eliminate their discrimination, as well as their greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth."

At that time, a fourth lotus suddenly appeared in the woman's right hand; she likewise cast that lotus toward the Tathāgata so that it reached the crown of the Buddha’s head, whereupon it immediately transformed into a fourth flower-canopy, adorned in the manner described above.
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!

By means of these roots of goodness, I pray that in future ages, if there are sentient beings dwelling in the four inversions, I may preach the Dharma for them so that they may eliminate those four inversions."
At that time, through the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, a fifth lotus suddenly appeared in her right hand.

The woman then took that flower and threw it toward the Tathāgata; when the flower arrived, it rested upon the crown of the Buddha's head and immediately became a fifth flower-canopy, its adornments being as described above.
At that time, the girl spoke again:
"World-Honored One!

By means of these roots of goodness, may I, in future lives, whenever there are sentient beings covered by the five hindrances, preach the Dharma for them so that they may eliminate those five hindrances."

At that time, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, a sixth lotus suddenly appeared in her right hand. The woman likewise took that lotus and threw it toward the Tathāgata; when the flower arrived, it rested upon the Buddha’s crown and transformed once more into a sixth flower-canopy, its adornments being as described above.
At that time, the woman spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
By means of these roots of goodness, may I, in future ages, for those sentient beings who are attached to the six sense bases, preach the Dharma so that they may be freed from such attachment."

At that time, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, a seventh lotus suddenly and spontaneously appeared in her right hand. The girl then again cast that flower toward the Tathāgata; upon reaching the Buddha’s crown, it immediately transformed into a seventh flower-canopy, its shape and size exactly as described above.
At that time, the girl spoke again:
“World-Honored One!

By means of the causes and conditions of these roots of goodness, may I, in a future age, whenever there are sentient beings dwelling in attachment to the seven consciousnesses, preach the Dharma for them so that they may sever and eliminate it.”

At that time, through the Buddha’s supernatural power, a sudden eighth lotus appeared in her right hand. The woman again held it toward the Buddha and cast it; once the flower arrived, it sequentially formed an eighth lotus-canopy, its dimensions and shape being as described above.
Thereupon, the girl spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
May I, in a future life, by virtue of this wholesome cause, preach the Dharma for any sentient beings who are attached to the eight inversions, so that they may all eliminate them."

At that time, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, a ninth lotus suddenly appeared in her right hand. The woman again hurled it from afar toward the crown of the Buddha’s head; once it arrived, it successively transformed into a ninth lotus canopy, the dimensions of which were as previously described.
Thereupon, the girl spoke again:
"World-Honored One!

By means of these roots of goodness and their causal conditions, may it be that in future ages, if there are sentient beings who abide in the nine latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), I shall preach the Dharma for them so that they may eliminate those nine latent tendencies."

At that time, through the Buddha’s supernatural power, a tenth lotus suddenly appeared in her right hand. The woman then threw that flower toward the crown of the Tathāgata’s head; once it arrived, it successively transformed into a tenth flower-canopy, adorned in length and breadth as previously described.
At that time, the girl spoke again:
"World-Honored One!

By means of these roots of goodness, may I in a future age be fully endowed with the ten powers, just as the World-Honored One now emits great light to illuminate the lands of the ten directions, without any difference."

At that time, the flower canopies manifested by them reached as high as the Brahma-heaven; because of those flower canopies, the sons of the gods dwelling on earth up to the Great Brahmā, together with immeasurable thousands of millions of celestial hosts, came to assemble there once again.
At that time, the World-Honored One smiled.

Now, it is the natural law of all Buddhas that when they smile, various colored rays of light issue from their mouths—namely, colors such as blue, yellow, red, white, and crystal, as well as colors such as gold and silver.

That light radiated forth, reaching immeasurable and boundless buddha-fields; it extended everywhere up to the Brahma heavens, eclipsing the sun and moon. Its brilliance and power were peerlessly magnificent, shining with dazzling splendor before returning to enter the crown of the Buddha's head.

At that time, the Elder Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and joined his palms together. With a verse, he asked the Buddha about the cause and conditions for his smile and the emission of light:
"All those who possess wisdom are not without eyes, And regarding all phenomena, they have no doubt;
The light that universally illuminates the world is impartial— What is the cause and condition for this smile?"
In past kalpas, you, O Honored One, practiced giving; Your pure conduct of precepts was like a precious jewel;
You dwelt in patience as immovable as Mount Sumeru— For what reason does the Honored One now smile with light?
Constantly cultivating diligence and meditative concentration, you have escaped the cycle of birth and death within the realms of existence;
your mental activity is profound and far-reaching like the ocean—what is the cause for your smile and the emission of light?
You constantly practice compassion without rest, and likewise with joy and equanimity;
you are able to rescue those who have lost their way—what is the cause for the Honored One’s smile and emission of light?
From a single pore of the Honored One’s body, light radiates forth, reaching throughout the infinite lands of the ten directions;
suddenly it eclipses the brilliance of the sun and moon, surpassing their power to become eyes for others.
The sounds he utters are wondrously pure, Possessing the sixty qualities, unique among the world’s honored ones;
All who hear them can never be satiated, And they are further able to extinguish all afflictions.
Regarding the immeasurable multitudes in the lands of the ten directions, and all those whose minds engage with various objects—
since the World-Honored One has known them and resolved their web of doubts, for what reason does the Honored One smile and emit light?
Who now resolutely gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment?
Who now mounts the Buddha’s vast Great Vehicle?
Who now thus fulfills the heart's vow?
The World-Honored One smiled and emitted light.
Who has now subdued the four kinds of Māras—namely, the Māra of afflictions, the Māra of death, the Māra of the aggregates, and the celestial Māra?
For what reason does he smile and emit this light?
World-Honored One, who now realizes the great benefit?
Who is the Dharma-abundant one, the lion among men?
Whose fame has reached the lands of the ten directions?
Such a smile and the emission of light—
O All-Knowing One, you who extinguish all unwholesomeness, whose loving-kindness is the most supreme among all acts of compassion,
and who have severed all conceptual constructions— what is the cause for this smile and the emission of light?
Who now has attained such vast benefit?
Who else now has fulfilled their heart's wish?
Who is it that has now harmonized with the Ten Powers?
Thus he emitted light and smiled.
Ten million devas in the sky, yakṣas, garuḍas, mahoragas, and various celestial maidens joined their palms in homage;
gazing up at the World-Honored One with hearts full of joy.
An immeasurable assembly of bodhisattvas has gathered, gazing up from all the lands of the ten directions;
they, whose profound wisdom is like the ocean, desire to hear the Dharma—what is the cause for this radiant smile on your pure countenance?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to Ānanda in verse:
“Ānanda, behold this young girl, With her ten fingers joined in palms together before me;
Having witnessed the wondrous supernatural powers of the Buddhas, She has immediately resolved upon supreme bodhicitta.”
In the past, I have seen three hundred Buddhas, those whom I have encountered throughout birth after birth;
in every life I have always shown them reverence and respect, constantly aspiring, "How may I realize Bodhi?"
May I not be born within the evil realms; may I be born only among devas and humans.
May I never forget the bodhicitta in whatever place I am born, and after the end of this life, may I know my past lives.
In the past, I saw the Tathāgata named Kāśyapa; While on an upper story, I threw my body down before him.
Because I made offerings to that venerable Kāśyapa, I have now attained non-arising and the patient acceptance of accordance with truth.
Furthermore, there was a Buddha named Kulu Village, to whom he offered a set of exquisite robes;
for this reason, he now possesses a golden body, pure and radiant like the moon deity.
There was a Buddha, Kāṇakamuni; I made offerings to him with incense, flowers, ointments, and powders.
Because of this, a wondrous fragrance issued from my mouth, like that of sandalwood or the utpala lotus.
The Buddha was named Śikhin, the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings; for seven full days he gazed up at that Honored One.
Therefore, his two eyes are the color of blue lotuses, such that all who behold them never grow weary of looking.
For five hundred lifetimes, he has felt weary of and detached from all desires, constantly practicing pure brahmacarya;
if anyone arises with desire to observe him, they shall attain a pure mind free from desire.
Therefore, having been born among the gods of the Thirty-three, he has come from there to be born into the Licchavi clan;
knowing his past conditions in all places of birth, he skillfully speaks these subtle and wondrous verses.
He teaches and transforms his parents and all his kinsmen, bringing benefit to immeasurable sentient beings;
desiring to inspire them toward enlightenment through such teaching, he is born into the noble and eminent Licchavi clan.
He taught and transformed maidens, boys, men, and women, causing them to enter the Buddha Vehicle;
twenty-three thousand types of human beings were brought to maturity on the path of immeasurable bodhi.
This woman shall transform her female body; before long she will renounce the world within my Dharma.
Having extensively practiced the pure and great Brahma-conduct, at the end of life here she will be reborn in heaven.
Having ended his life according to the mandate of heaven, he was reborn here;
in future evil ages, he shall protect my Dharma, bring benefit to these multitudes, and upon relinquishing his life, be reborn once more in Tuṣita.
When Maitreya descends to be born in the future, he will become the son of King Śaṅkha of the Cakravartin lineage;
among the many arts and skills of that time, he will be pleasing, upright, and endowed with all virtues.
Having made offerings to that Honored One for three months, along with the assembly surrounding him on all sides,
he went forth as a monk in the presence of that Buddha, followed by a multitude of six thousand three hundred.
Having upheld the true Dharma of that Buddha, one will thereafter be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss;
having attained rebirth there to behold Amitābha, one shall pay homage with reverence and make offerings.
Throughout the buddha-fields of this Auspicious Aeon, And in all worlds throughout the ten directions,
As well as for the Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, May you bring benefit to all those multitudes.
With the power of diligence, wisdom, and meditative concentration, they made offerings to such World-Honored Ones;
having made offerings to the Buddhas throughout kalpas, they transformed and guided immeasurable thousands of millions of beings.
After eighty thousand koṭis of eons, he shall become a Buddha named Candrottara;
that Honored One named Candrottara will emit a wondrous light from the white tuft between his eyebrows.
That golden light was exceedingly brilliant and beautiful, Its radiant splendor illuminating that buddha-field everywhere;
The light of the sun, moon, fire, and mani-jewels, As well as the lights of all the stars, were all made to disappear.
Day and night, years and months, as well as the four seasons, all arise from that light and nothing else;
in that land, there shall be no pratyekabuddhas, nor even the names of śrāvakas or arhats.
The assembly of pure and courageous Bodhisattvas—such shall be that Honored One alone;
the bodies of those in his assembly are all golden in color, adorned with the full array of hundreds of marks.
All are called "Sublime and Delightful Humans," for in that land there are none born from desire or from a womb;
they are spontaneously born within the calyxes of lotuses, and upon birth, they possess great majesty and virtue.
Incalculable among all reckonings, with immeasurable supernormal powers reaching all lands;
they possess the dharma of non-arising patience without obstruction.
In those lands there are no Māras or heterodox teachers, nor are there any who break the precepts or evil companions; they receive pure retribution as if in Tuṣita Heaven.
If there are those born in that land, all their karmic retributions shall be entirely equal;
nets of exquisite gold, silver, and pearls will spread widely, covering that entire world.
That Great World-Honored One’s lifespan was long; he remained in the world for seventy-three thousand kalpas.
After his life ended and he entered parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma remained in the world for a full kalpa.
Whether that Honored One was in the world or had passed away, the Dharma teaching remained the same without distinction.
If I were to praise for an eon all the merits of the World-Honored One’s buddha-field,
it would be like taking a single drop of water from the great ocean— just as the various metaphors spoken today.

At that time, Candrottarā, having heard from the Buddha’s presence that she had been granted the prophecy, was filled with immeasurable joy and leaped for gladness; she soared into the air, rising to a height of seven tala trees above the ground.
Once they had stayed there for seven *tāla* trees' height, that girl immediately transformed her female body into that of a man.
At that moment, the great earth shook in its entirety, a great sound resounded, a rain of celestial flowers fell, and a great radiance shone forth, illuminating the entire world.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Candrottara stood in mid-air and praised the Buddha with these verses:
"Even if Mount Sumeru were to shake and the sky were to fall to earth, If the abodes of the asuras were all utterly destroyed,
If the great ocean were to dry up and the moon-god were to fall— The Tathāgata would never utter a false word."
Even if the multitudes of the ten directions were to unite their minds, such that fire might become water or water might become fire;
the One of Greatest Honor with immeasurable merit remains without contradiction in his purpose: to benefit all sentient beings.
The great earth and empty space become a chaotic void; a hundred lands enter together into a single mustard seed.
A net may be used to bind a fierce wind, yet the Tathāgata never utters a false word.
Since the World-Honored One has spoken these words of truth, I shall resolutely abide in the path to Bodhi;
now that the great earth trembles everywhere, there is no doubt that I shall realize Bodhi.
Now that I have received the prophecy of enlightenment, I shall turn the wheel of Dharma without distinction;
just as the World-Honored One has taught the Dharma, so have I already heard it throughout hundreds of kalpas.
To benefit the eight classes of devas and humans, as well as the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus and others;
and for the sake of immeasurable bodhisattvas—do not harbor doubts regarding the Buddha.
In the future, all shall become non-conceptual; therefore, one must resolutely resolve upon the Bodhicitta.
All phenomena are entirely like illusions and transformations; what the Buddhas have taught is like a dream.
In this state, there is no person and no nourisher; No sentient beings, no life-force, and no *pudgala*.
The intrinsic nature of all such phenomena Is no different from the analogy of empty space.
All the female bodies I previously possessed—those bodies are empty in essence and lack reality.
Since they have no substantial reality, they are empty; being empty in essence, they are devoid of substance and cannot be grasped.
Those bodies arise from inverted conceptualization, and such conceptualization is like a bird flying through the sky.
Desiring to accomplish the Buddha-bodhi, Furthermore desiring to subdue the hosts of the four Māras,
And furthermore desiring that within the trichiliocosm, The subtle and wondrous Great Dharma-wheel be turned.
You all must vigorously resolve upon Bodhicitta and reverently make offerings to the Bhagavān;
before long, you shall achieve the state of the Honored One of Merit, identical to the True Body without any distinction.
I pay homage with my head to the Śramaṇa, the Honored One among superior men, the most venerable among those who possess two feet;
he who can bestow beloved things always gains what is loved, and by bestowing the wealth of the Dharma, he attains sovereignty.
The Buddha is the source of bliss and can bestow it; he can subdue enemies and all Māras.
I praise the Most Victorious Honored One who deserves praise, and I praise the Sovereign who has no envy.
In all directions that I observe with my mind, may I behold the inconceivable Buddhas emitting light just as the Lion of the Śākyas does now;
may I likewise come to know the Buddhas of the ten directions.
All are of the same essence, awakening to the single Dharma; within the dharma of True Suchness, there is no duality.
All immeasurable sentient beings share the same ultimate reality; one who possesses such patience shall become a Buddha.
When the Bodhisattva Candrottara had spoken these verses, he descended from the air and prostrated himself with his head at [the Buddha's] feet.
As he was prostrating, before his head had even touched the ground, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas appeared before his eyes.
Those Buddhas, with one voice, bestowed upon that Candrottara the prediction that he would attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

When the Bodhisattva Candrottara saw with his own eyes those hundreds of thousands of Buddhas bestowing the prediction upon him, joy and exultation filled his entire being such that he could not contain himself; he immediately requested ordination from the Tathāgata, saying:
"Excellent!"
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me ordination within the Dharma you yourself have taught.
The Buddha then addressed the Bodhisattva Candrottarā:
"If this is indeed certain, you should ask your parents whether they have given their consent.
At that time, the boy’s parents, having witnessed such a display of miraculous power and having heard the Buddha bestow a prediction of enlightenment upon him, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So be it, World-Honored One!"
We have already given our consent;
we only pray that the World-Honored One will allow him to go forth into homelessness!
"Furthermore, we vow that in future ages we shall encounter such a Dharma as this.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately permitted the youth to go forth.
When the youth went forth, twelve thousand people together resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

When the Buddha had spoken this fundamental teaching of the Dharma, there were another seventy *nayutas* of devas and humans who became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure eye regarding all phenomena;
furthermore, five hundred bhikṣus attained the exhaustion of outflows within the unconditioned Dharma and their minds were liberated;
and there were two hundred bhikṣuṇīs together with twenty thousand of their peers, some of whom had not yet resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, but likewise gave rise to the bodhicitta.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Bodhisattva Candrottara, the Elder Ānanda, the assembly of bodhisattvas, and the great multitude of gods, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and the other eight classes of beings, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Girl Candrottarā, Scroll II.
